classification.difficultyReason: Organise raw golf scores into frequencies and construct an equally spaced dot plot that preserves gaps between scores. Identifying the highest and most frequent scores requires direct comparisons, with the table explicitly requested first.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 applies the frequency-table method of Example 1 and the dot-plot construction demonstrated on page 4; identifying the largest and most frequent score uses the same data.
questions.methodNote: Count repeated values in a frequency table, including unused intermediate values, then stack one dot per observation above an equally spaced numerical axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count repeated scores, identify the maximum and most frequent score, and construct a dot plot.

classification.difficultyReason: Count repeated organism totals, include unused intermediate values and transfer the frequencies to a labelled dot plot. The requested frequency table scaffolds the representation change using the taught procedure.

questions.mappingNote: The droplet counts use the same frequency-table and ungrouped dot-plot methods as Examples 1 and 2.
questions.methodNote: Record the number of occurrences of every integer value in the range and represent each observation with one vertically stacked dot.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Organise 23 observations into a frequency table and construct a dot plot with zero-frequency gaps.

classification.difficultyReason: Link rounded handspan measurements to a self-organised frequency table and choose an axis covering the collected data. Then identify extremes and the most common length and construct the dot plot; the measurement procedure and sequence are supplied.

questions.mappingNote: The activity combines page 2 measurement conventions with the page 3 frequency-table method and page 4 dot plots. The requested extreme and most common lengths are read from the collected data.
questions.methodNote: Collect measurement data with units and stated precision, tally observations into a frequency table, and construct a dot plot with one dot per observation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect class measurements, organise variable data, identify extreme and most frequent lengths, and construct a dot plot.

classification.difficultyReason: Independently count repeated wire lengths and choose a workable numerical scale across their range, preserving unequal gaps between observed lengths. Link those frequencies to dot stacks without an intermediate table being requested.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly assesses constructing a dot plot from raw numerical measurements; finding the mode is not requested.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 define a dot plot as one dot per observation, stacked above its numerical value. Page 7 Example 4 demonstrates counting frequencies and constructing the labelled dot plot.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a dot plot from 21 measurements using an evenly spaced numerical scale with gaps between observed values.

classification.difficultyReason: Count entries and identify the most frequent value in a supplied stem-and-leaf plot.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 8–9 explain reading individual stem-and-leaf entries and finding modes from repeated entries. Pages 5–6 define the mode through frequency. These methods directly support counting buses and identifying 38 as the most frequent passenger count.
questions.methodNote: Each stem-and-leaf entry represents one observation. Combine the tens stem with the units leaf to read a value; the mode is the value with the highest frequency.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count entries and identify the most frequent value in a supplied stem-and-leaf plot.

classification.difficultyReason: Organise thirty two- and three-digit observations into an ordered stem-and-leaf plot and identify two modes.

questions.mappingNote: Marianthi's text-message task directly parallels Example 5's daily email counts, including three-digit values and two modes.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–9 teach stems formed from all digits before the final digit, ordered leaves and repeated leaves. Example 5 identifies two modes from equal highest frequencies. Pages 5–6 define mode as the most frequent value.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Organise thirty two- and three-digit observations into an ordered stem-and-leaf plot and identify two modes.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses the mean and total to determine the unknown number of observations.

questions.mappingNote: The closest catalogue skill is find-value-from-mean because the question requires recovering an unknown quantity from a given mean and total. The authored inverse-operation solution is mathematically correct, but original teaching evidence for that inverse method remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 defines mean as the sum of the values divided by the number of values. Pages 12–14 demonstrate forward mean calculations. None of these inspected pages demonstrates reversing the formula to determine the number of observations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses the mean and total to determine the unknown number of observations.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct the ordered stem-and-leaf representation, then locate and highlight the twelfth observation as the median, linking two explicitly requested methods.

questions.mappingNote: The question combines construction of the taught stem-and-leaf display with identifying the median directly in that display.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 uses tens digits as stems and ordered units digits as leaves. Page 10 defines the median as the middle ordered value for an odd-sized dataset.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct an ordered stem-and-leaf plot and identify its middle observation.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines mean, median and mode constraints to reconstruct five positive whole numbers.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly combines mean, median and mode. Its solution also reverses the mean calculation to obtain the total; taught-method acceptance remains unresolved.
questions.methodNote: Pages 5–6 define mode as the most frequent value; pages 10–11 explain ordering and the middle value for the median; pages 11–14 define and demonstrate mean as sum divided by number of values. These pages do not demonstrate reconstructing a dataset from simultaneous summary-statistic constraints.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines mean, median and mode constraints to reconstruct five positive whole numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Organise 42 three-digit measurements into an ordered stem-and-leaf plot, then identify the middle pair and extremes.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly applies the three-digit stem-and-leaf method in Example 5. Part b applies the even-number median method in Example 6 to the ordered plot. Part c applies the range definition. Representing the dataset is the principal assessed construction.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–9 teach stems formed from all digits except the final units digit and ordered leaves. Pages 10–11 teach averaging the two middle ordered values for an even dataset. Page 14 defines range as largest minus smallest.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Organise 42 three-digit measurements into an ordered stem-and-leaf plot, then identify the middle pair and extremes.

classification.difficultyReason: Count each absence value and place the corresponding stack of dots above a labelled numerical axis, directly applying the taught representation.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly applies the taught dot-plot construction to a single dataset of integer absence counts.
questions.methodNote: The dot-plot definition on page 3 and plots on page 4 represent each observation by one dot and stack repeated values vertically above a labelled numerical axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count repeated integer values and represent their frequencies with vertically stacked dots.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct calculation of three summary statistics from two numerical data sets.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly apply these three methods to raw numerical lists; no frequency table or graphical construction is required.
questions.methodNote: Pages 10–11 teach ordering the data and averaging the two middle values for an even-sized set. Pages 11–12 teach dividing the sum by the number of values. Page 14 defines range as largest minus smallest.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct calculation of three summary statistics from two numerical data sets.

classification.difficultyReason: Read values from a stem-and-leaf plot, calculate their mean and locate the median.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 8–9 explain stem-and-leaf notation. Pages 10–11 teach the middle-value median, and pages 11–12 teach the sum-divided-by-count mean. These directly support both requested calculations.
questions.methodNote: Read each stem as the tens digit and each leaf as the units digit. Divide the sum of all values by their count for the mean; select the middle ordered value for an odd-sized dataset.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read values from a stem-and-leaf plot, calculate their mean and locate the median.

classification.difficultyReason: Interprets a supplied two-digit-leaf key, counts observations in an interval and locates the middle of 25 ordered values.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced assessed operation is finding the median. Counting leaves and decoding the explicitly supplied key support interpretation of the given plot; no construction of a new two-digit-leaf plot is required.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–9 explain ordered leaves and stems. Question 6 itself supplies the two-digit-leaf key. Pages 10–11 define the median as the middle ordered value for an odd number of observations; page 14 demonstrates locating that middle value.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interprets a supplied two-digit-leaf key, counts observations in an interval and locates the middle of 25 ordered values.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the preceding two-digit-leaf convention to construct the plot, then use grouped counts to answer the interval question and locate the thirteenth observation for the median.

questions.mappingNote: Part a assesses representing numerical data with a stem-and-leaf plot; b interprets the grouped observations; c and d calculate median and range. The plot uses the representation supplied immediately before this question and confirmed by the matching answer, pending independent taught-method review.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–9 demonstrate ordered stem-and-leaf plots with single-digit leaves. Question 6 on page 17 supplies the two-digit-leaf key 7 | 24 means 724. Pages 10–11 and 14 teach the median as the middle ordered observation; page 14 teaches range as maximum minus minimum. No attached standalone teaching demonstrates constructing a plot with two-digit leaves.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct an ordered plot using two-digit leaves, count observations in an interval, and find the median and range.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover a missing observation from the mean, then order the completed dataset to find its median.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses finding a missing value from a given mean; part b applies the demonstrated even-sized median method to the completed dataset. Part a requires additional original taught-method evidence before content acceptance.
questions.methodNote: Pages 11 and 13 define the mean as the sum divided by the number of values. Pages 10–11 demonstrate ordering an even-sized dataset and averaging its two middle values. The inspected originals do not demonstrate reversing the mean formula to recover a missing observation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover a missing observation from the mean, then order the completed dataset to find its median.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover the maximum from the range, carry it into the known-value total, and reverse the mean calculation to find the missing observation by subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses the range to recover the maximum; part b selects the fifth ordered observation; part c uses the given mean to recover the total and subtract the known observations. Finding a missing value from the mean is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 10–11 teach the middle-value method for the median. Pages 11, 13–14 state and apply mean = sum of values divided by number of values. Page 14 defines range as the difference between the largest and smallest observations. These pages do not explicitly demonstrate finding a missing observation by reversing the mean calculation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines the range and ordered median with finding a missing observation from the mean.
